newsitem.title: USA: Irish president dedicates memorial to Great Famine.
newsitem.headline: Irish president dedicates memorial to Great Famine.

text.p: Irish President Mary Robinson on Wednesday dedicated the first U.S. memorial to The Great Famine, paying homage to the millions who died and were displaced 150 years ago and urging an end to famines today.
"This is a very special memorial to An Gorta Mor - The Great Famine," Robinson told the 1,000 or so onlookers.

"What would those desperate people who caught the coffin ships and came to this country have thought? 1847 was the worst year of The Great Famine. And here we are in July of 1997 and here I am as president of Ireland unveiling on Cambridge Commons...a memorial to The Great Famine," she said.

Some 30 years ago as a student at nearby Harvard University, Robinson was inspired by the U.S. civil rights movement and returned to Ireland to became one of its leading civil rights lawyers, championing the right to contraception and divorce. A small group of anti-abortion protesters held up signs saying, "Mary Robinson's Famine Abortion" as she spoke.

The $100,000 memorial, crafted by Irish artist Maurice Harron, depicts a mother and her dead child. It was funded by "both Irish and non-Irish -- the honorary Irish" in Cambridge, said John O'Connor, co-founder of the Irish Famine Committee.
The statue is dedicated not only to those who died in The Great Famine, but also "to the millions of people who go to bed hungry every night," said John Flaherty, co-founder of the committee.
Indeed, Robinson noted, "I wish we could say as a people that in a world of plenty, there would be no famine. But look at North Korea today. There is famine in our world. There is malnutrition."

At least a million people died in the famine which lasted from 1845 to 1850. O'Connor said it was decisions by London based on supporting free market forces rather than intervening directly to aid the starving that exacerbated the tragedy and caused people to flee the country.

Earlier this year, Robinson led a famine commemoration at which new British Prime Minister Tony Blair issued a message, telling the Irish people: "That one million people should have died in what was then part of the richest and most powerful nation in the world is something that still causes pain."
